turns.content: My wedding is six weeks away. My closest friend Rohan is supposed to be in my haldi and give a toast — he's been my guy since first year of college. But every time I bring up his travel from Bangalore he just says "let's see, I'll definitely try." Should I just book his flight myself and be done with it?

Oh I feel this in my chest — six weeks out and you need to *know* if your college brother is gonna be there for your haldi and your toast. Those aren't filler roles, that's core memory stuff.

But "let's see, I'll definitely try" after all these years? That's vague in a way that stings a little, right?

Before you book the flight, maybe have one straight conversation with him. Not about logistics — about the truth. Something like: *"Rohan, I'm locking in the haldi plan and I really want you there. Is something holding you back — money, work, something else? Because if you can't make it, I'd rather know now than keep hoping."*

Sometimes "let's see" actually means "I can't afford the ticket and I'm too embarrassed to say it" or "my job's a nightmare and I don't want to lie." If that's it, *then* offering to book it is the most loving thing ever. But if you just book it blind, you might put him in an awkward spot or end up out the cash.

You deserve a yes or a no from your closest friend. He owes you that clarity.

I checked, flights are like nine thousand return. Not crazy. He switched jobs a couple of months back, some startup. And lately his replies are two words where he used to send voice notes. I'm telling myself he's busy but it's been weeks of this.

Nine thousand isn't nothing, but it's not the kind of money that should block your closest friend from your haldi. So it's probably not the ticket.

And the two-word replies where there used to be voice notes — that's the part that would worry me more than the travel. That's a temperature drop. Startup jobs can absolutely swallow a person whole, especially in the first few months when they're trying to prove themselves. But weeks of bare-minimum replies from someone who was your person? That hurts, and you're allowed to feel that even if you're telling yourself "he's just busy."

Here's what I'd do before booking anything: send him one real message that isn't about the wedding at all. Something like *"Rohan, you've been quiet for weeks and I'm lowkey worried. The new job eating you alive? I miss our actual conversations."* No ask, no logistics. Just see if he's okay.

Because if he's drowning in the startup and barely keeping his head up, booking a flight and needing a toast from him might be the last thing he can handle — and he might not know how to tell you. And if he replies with another "all good bro" and nothing more... then you'll know this isn't about the job. You'll know something in the friendship shifted, and you can plan your wedding heart with eyes open.

Either way, you need the truth from him before you spend the money or the emotional energy.

Honestly it's starting to hurt now. If he actually cared he would have just said yes on day one, no? I'm thinking I should just call him tonight and ask him straight — "bro, are you coming or not, yes or no." At least I'll know where I stand.

Yeah, call him. You've been patient for weeks and the not-knowing is worse than a no at this point — at least a no lets you grieve it and move on with your planning.

But one thing before you dial: try not to go in with "if he cared he'd have said yes on day one" as the verdict. Sometimes people we love go weird and silent precisely *because* they care and feel like they're falling short. The new job, the short replies — could be he's ashamed he can't show up the way he wants to. Or yeah, could be the friendship just isn't what it was.

Either way, the call is right. Just ask him straight like you said — "bro, are you coming or not?" And then *listen* to what he actually says, not just whether it's the answer you wanted. If he gives you a real reason, you'll know. If he gives you another "let's see," that *is* your answer, and you can stop twisting yourself up over it.

You deserve friends at your wedding who want to be there. If Rohan's one of them, he'll say so tonight.

My fiancée says I'm overthinking and he's probably just swamped. But this is the same guy who took an overnight bus to be at my sister's wedding in 2019. Something has changed and I can't figure out what, and I hate that I'm angry at him two weeks before my haldi.

Your fiancée means well, but she wasn't there in 2019 — you were. The overnight bus guy doesn't go quiet on something this big because he's "just swamped." Swamped people still say *"man I'm buried but I wouldn't miss it, count me in."* That's the difference. So no, you're not overthinking. You're reading the room correctly. Something *has* changed, and you not knowing what is exactly why it's eating at you.

And that anger you're carrying two weeks before your haldi? That's the worst part, right? You don't want to be mad at your oldest friend during what's supposed to be a happy countdown. But you're not angry because you're petty — you're angry because you loved the version of him that showed up without being asked, and this new version feels like a stranger who won't even explain himself.

The call tonight is the only way to get your peace back. Not just for the headcount — for *you*, so you're not walking into your haldi with this knot in your chest. Whatever he says, at least it'll be the truth instead of a guess.

And hey — being angry doesn't make you a bad friend or a bad groom. It makes you someone who valued the friendship enough to notice it slipping.
